source.title: Discover-then-Name: Task-Agnostic Concept Bottlenecks via Automated Concept Discovery
source.authors: Sukrut Rao; S. Mahajan; Moritz Böhle; B. Schiele

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps SAE sparsity and measures reconstruction error, bearing on whether training choices affect the error; it does not analyze the error structure using the original claim’s measures.
record.gate_note: The study reports that increasing the L1 sparsity coefficient makes representations sparser but increases representation error (Fig. B1). SAE and classifier hyperparameter choices used to select configurations, and the CBM classification and intervention results, do not independently test the other dark-matter versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs on CLIP image embeddings to build concept bottleneck models and reports the CBMs' accuracy and interpretability. Its one error-related result is the L1 sweep in Fig. B1: higher λ1 gives sparser codes with higher reconstruction error. That is the standard sparsity–reconstruction trade-off, reported to characterise the tool and guide hyperparameter choice. It does not decompose the error, test its linear predictability, scaling, effect on loss or functional role, or ask whether the error shrinks with better architectures or objectives rather than reflecting the model's representation. So no version is tested, including V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that SAEs discover semantically consistent, automatically nameable concepts in CLIP and yield performant, interpretable task-agnostic CBMs. They propose larger SAEs and datasets as future work and draw no conclusion about SAE error structure.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAEs to discover visual concepts in CLIP and reports a sparsity–reconstruction-error tradeoff; it does not perform the dark-matter analyses in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reconstruction-error/sparsity tradeoff changes with the L1 sparsity coefficient.

fits_no_version.finding: In CLIP ResNet-50 SAEs trained on CC3M, a higher L1 coefficient λ1 gives sparser concept codes but higher reconstruction error (Fig. B1, qualitative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction error trades off against sparsity as the L1 coefficient varies (generic sparsity–fidelity trade-off) in vision-model SAEs.

record.problems: The relevant reconstruction-error result is described qualitatively, with numerical values only in a figure; the study does not assess error predictability, per-token patterns, or alternative SAE architectures/training methods.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results were found that measure the dark-matter error properties in the claim. CBM classification and concept-intervention results concern the trained bottleneck, not the SAE error term.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from input activations; not examined.
Per-token error-norm predictability, shared failure contexts across SAE sizes, persistence with scale; expansion factors 2/4/8 were swept, but no error results are reported by size.

Downstream harm of substituting SAE reconstructions compared with random errors of the same size; not measured. Zero-shot accuracy on reconstructions was used only to select an SAE, and no values are reported.
Linear versus nonlinear error components; not examined.
Whether SAE-feature analyses lose behaviour without the error term. The CBMs drop the error term, but no comparison with the error term kept is made.
Whether dark matter shrinks with better architectures, objectives or end-to-end training, or reflects training artifacts; only an L1 sweep within one architecture is shown.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V6 supports label is overturned. A within-architecture L1 sweep showing the usual sparsity–error trade-off is a selection and characterisation result for the study's tool. It does not test whether dark matter is a training artifact. The CBM classification and Waterbirds intervention results concern the bottleneck classifier, not the SAE error term.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of the SAE error vector is linearly predictable from input activations.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap in contexts where different sizes fail, and whether error vanishes with scale.
Whether SAE reconstruction replacement harms model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether the linear component represents unlearned features and the nonlinear component is qualitatively different or resists further dictionary learning.
Whether analyses based on SAE features lose model behaviour unless the error term is retained.

The study tests the effect of the sparsity penalty on reconstruction error, but does not establish that dark matter mostly reflects training choices, test shrinkage, dead latents or alternative objectives, or compare improved architectures or end-to-end training.

rows.subject: CLIP ResNet-50 SAE
rows.operation_detail: Varied the SAE L1 sparsity coefficient and measured reconstruction error and sparsity.
rows.measure: Representation reconstruction error and number of concepts used
rows.value: Higher λ1 yields sparser concept representations but higher representation error.
rows.note: The text describes the overall trend; individual numerical values are shown only in the figure. The result shows dependence on the sparsity penalty, not that training choices account for most error.
rows.check: This is an L1 hyperparameter sweep for selecting the SAE (a tool-characterisation result). A sparsity–error trade-off within one architecture cannot show whether dark matter is mostly a training artifact versus model structure, so it should not be linked to V6. The values appear only in the figure, with no baseline.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Reconstruction error rises as the L1 sparsity coefficient increases, showing that this training choice affects the error (R1); the broader artifact claim is not established.
